summary: SowSmart is a tool that helps farmers anywhere on Earth compare crop rotations for their own field using NASA Earth observations. A farmer points to their land, checks what the satellites see (when the field sits bare, the driest soil months, rain, heat, frost, slope and soil) and corrects anything wrong. Then they answer some questions, each of which accepts “I don’t know”. SowSmart compares their current rotation with three alternatives on a 12-month calendar: fill the bare window with a legume, break the pest cycle, or save water. It suggests only crops already grown in their country. Each option explains why it was suggested, its evidence, benefits, risks, information gaps and questions for a local expert, in plain language, in up to two languages, with a printable PDF. They can also get alerts for storms, floods, fires, heavy rain, dry soil and pest-favoring weather. A rules-based engine makes every recommendation from NASA data; AI only explains it, and every number is checked. SowSmart puts free NASA data to work for smallholders while supporting, never replacing, farmer judgment.
details:
What it does:

  • A free, mobile-first tool that helps farmers anywhere on Earth compare crop rotations for their own field using NASA data.
  • Find your land: use your location, tap a point, draw the field, or browse NASA satellite maps.
  • What the satellites see: bare months, driest soil months, rain, heat, frost, slope and soil. The farmer can correct any card.
  • Results: the current rotation vs. three alternatives on a 12-month calendar (fill the bare window, break the pest cycle, save water).
  • Each option explains: why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, risks, information gaps and questions for a local expert.
  • Alerts: storms, floods, fires, heavy rain, dry soil and pest-favoring weather near saved fields.

How it works

  • NASA data (POWER, SMAP, MODIS, GPM IMERG, GRACE-FO, SRTM, EONET, FIRMS, GIBS) is processed per field with Google Earth Engine.
  • A rules-based engine scores each option on water, soil, erosion, pests, weather risk, income and labor, weighted by the farmer’s goals.
  • Suggestions only include crops already grown in the farmer’s country (FAO data).
  • AI (Grok) only explains the results in plain words. It never decides, and every number it writes is checked.

Benefits

  • Free NASA data made usable for farmers of every resource level.
  • Shows when soil sits bare and which seasons are risky.
  • Points to ways to save water, build soil, break pest cycles or add income.
  • Every number traces back to its dataset.

Intended impact

  • Healthier soil: farmers see when their field sits bare and can fill those months with legumes or cover crops. That protects soil from erosion, adds nitrogen and organic matter, and helps rain soak in instead of running off.
  • Resilience to changing weather: frost, heat, dry spells and heavy-rain seasons are shown on the farmer’s own crop calendar. Farmers can choose rotations that avoid their riskiest months instead of finding out at harvest.
  • Resilience to changing water: rotations are compared on how much water they need versus what rain and soil provide, so farmers can pick options that hold up in drier years.
  • Fewer pests and more income: it shows chances to break pest cycles by changing plant families and to add a sellable crop in idle months.
  • Warnings: alerts for storms, floods, fires, heavy rain, dry soil and pest-favoring weather give farmers time to protect their fields.
  • Better decisions, not replaced ones: every option comes with its evidence, risks, information gaps and questions for a local expert. Farmers and extension workers make better-informed choices together.
  • Who it reaches: smallholders in remote areas, like our demo farm in Tagum City, Philippines, who rarely get this kind of analysis. The tool is free, in their language, and their report can be saved as a PDF to use offline.

What we considered

  • Remote areas: farmers often have weak or no internet, so reports can be exported as a PDF to save, print or share over messaging apps. The app is also light enough for slow connections.
  • Language: many farmers don’t speak English, so reports come in widely spoken farming languages: Spanish, French, Portuguese, Hindi, Swahili and Tagalog, plus English (up to two per report).
  • Every resource level: advice fits hand tools through full machinery, and nothing is assumed when information is missing.
  • Honest limits: confidence labels, “conditions favor” wording for pest alerts, and a warning that non-English reports may be less precise.
  • Privacy: only the owner sees their farm location, and it is never sent to the AI.
  • Farmer judgment first: the tool supports farmers and local experts and never replaces them.

How it’s creative

  • Hand Drawn Farm Land Farmers can trace their exact field boundary on the map, so the satellite analysis covers their land rather than a generic grid square.
  • It finds the field’s empty months from space. Years of NASA greenness data (MODIS NDVI) show when the field sits bare. SowSmart fills that gap with a legume or cover crop, so idle months become soil building or extra income.
  • The farmer can correct the satellites. Most tools hand down a satellite answer. SowSmart asks “Is this right?” on every estimate, and the farmer’s corrections change the scores. NASA data and local knowledge decide together.
  • AI that can’t make things up. Most AI farm advisors let the AI decide. In SowSmart, a transparent engine makes every recommendation from data, AI only puts it in plain words, and any number not in the data is rejected automatically.
  • Neighbors are warned together. When NASA tracks a storm, flood or fire, every farmer with a saved field in its path gets an alert, not just the one who checked. A satellite event becomes a community early-warning network.
  • Advice a farmer can actually follow. It only suggests crops already grown in the farmer’s country (FAO data), so seed, know-how and buyers exist locally. This matters because generic “ideal crop” lists often aren’t practical.
  • It works with nothing to start from. A new farmer with no crops and no details still gets starting options for their land, and nothing is assumed about them.
  • Built for the farmer’s reality: reports in their own language with scientific terms explained in plain words, and a PDF that works offline and can be shared by phone.

TECH STACK:

Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL

Backend: FastAPI, Google Earth Engine, NASA POWER API, Matplotlib

Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Terra Draw, Turf

Services:

TigerData (Postgres, TimescaleDB, PostGIS)

xAI Grok API

Auth0 (sign-in)

Web Push and email (alerts)

Cloudflare Tunnel and Pages (hosting)
